questions.question: What is the String pool in Java?
questions.title: What Is the String Pool in Java?
questions.direct_answer: The String pool (also called the string intern pool) is a special area in the JVM heap where String literals are stored and reused. When you write `String s = "hello"`, the JVM checks if `"hello"` already exists in the pool — if yes, it returns the same object instead of creating a new one. This saves memory when the same string value appears many times.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand where string literals live in memory and why the JVM can safely share them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking all Strings go into the pool. Only literals and interned strings go there. `new String('hello')` bypasses the pool and always creates a new heap object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the pool is only safe because Strings are immutable — if one variable could modify 'hello', every other variable pointing to the same pooled object would be corrupted. Immutability and the pool are inseparable.

sections.title: One Copy of Each Literal, Shared Across the Program
sections.content:
The String pool is a special area of memory where Java stores and reuses `String` literals so identical text isn't duplicated.

Why does Java bother? Strings are everywhere in a typical program — names, keys, messages, labels — and the same text shows up over and over. Without the pool, every `"hello"` in your code would be its own object, wasting memory on identical content.

How it works: when you write `String s = "hello"`, the JVM looks in the pool first. If `"hello"` is already there, it hands back the **same object**; if not, it creates one and stores it. This automatic reuse is called **interning**. Because both variables end up pointing to one object, `==` — which compares addresses — returns `true` for two equal literals.

```java
String s1 = "hello";
String s2 = "hello";
System.out.println(s1 == s2); // true — same pooled object
```

The nuance: the pool only holds literals and strings you explicitly `intern()`. A `new String("hello")` skips the pool entirely and builds a fresh object on the regular heap, so `s1 == s3` is `false` even though the text matches.

The gotcha worth remembering: this sharing is only safe because `String` is **immutable**. Nobody can change the pooled `"hello"`, so no variable can corrupt another's view. Since Java 7 the pool lives in the normal heap, so unreferenced pooled strings can even be garbage-collected.

sections.title: Pool Sharing vs new String — the == Difference
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking every `String` lives in the pool** — only literals and strings you explicitly `intern()` are pooled; `new String("hello")`, concatenation results, and strings from input or files land on the regular heap.
- **Comparing content with `==`** — `==` checks whether two references point to the same object, not whether the characters match; it returns `true` for two literals by luck of pooling and `false` for a `new String`. Use `.equals()`.
- **Assuming `new String("hello")` holds different text** — the content is identical to the literal; only the object identity differs, which is exactly why `==` and `.equals()` disagree.
- **Believing the pool still lives in PermGen** — since Java 7 it sits in the normal heap, so pooled strings are subject to garbage collection like any other object.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One object per unique literal** — the pool stores a single copy of each distinct `String` literal, so `"hello" == "hello"` is `true` because both references point to the same pooled object.
- **Interning is automatic for literals** — every literal in your source is pooled at class-load time without you calling anything; `String.intern()` is only needed to pool a runtime-built string manually.
- **`new String("hello")` always bypasses the pool** — it forces a brand-new heap object, so `s1 == s3` is `false` even though `s1.equals(s3)` is `true`.
- **Immutability is what makes sharing safe** — because no one can mutate the pooled `"hello"`, many variables share it with zero risk of one corrupting another; the pool could not exist without it.
- **Use `.equals()` for content, `==` for identity** — `==` compares addresses, so relying on it for `String` content is a bug that passes for literals and fails for everything else.
- **Since Java 7 the pool lives in the heap** — moved out of PermGen, so pooled strings can be garbage-collected and no longer cause `PermGen` out-of-memory errors.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Here's the mental model I use: the same literal text in Java is stored once and shared, not copied. So when I write `"hello"` in two places, both variables actually point to the exact same object in a region called the string pool — that's why `==` returns `true` for them. The JVM does this automatically; it's called **interning**.

Where people trip up is assuming that holds for every `String`. It doesn't. The moment you write `new String("hello")`, you force a fresh object on the heap that skips the pool, so `==` against the literal is now `false` even though the characters are identical. That's the whole reason the rule exists: compare `String` content with **`.equals()`**, never `==`. `==` asks 'same object?', `.equals()` asks 'same characters?' — and for strings you almost always mean the second.

The thing I'd add to stand out is why the pool is even safe to do. It only works because `String` is **immutable**. If you could change the pooled `"hello"` to `"world"`, every other variable sharing that object would silently break. Immutability and the pool are inseparable — one enables the other. So my position: lean on the pool as an optimization, but never let your correctness depend on `==` — always reach for `.equals()`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `String s = "hello"` and `String s = new String("hello")` in Java?
questions.title: String Literal vs new String() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `String s = "hello"` uses the String pool — the JVM checks if `"hello"` already exists there and reuses it if so. `String s = new String("hello")` always creates a brand new String object on the heap, bypassing the pool entirely. The content is the same; the object identity (`==`) is different.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the memory and identity implications of using a literal vs constructor, and can explain why == gives different results in each case.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare a literal and a new String() and expecting true — they are different objects even if the content is identical.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that `new String('hello')` is almost never the right choice in production code — the only reason you'd use it is if you have a very long char array and want a String from a small slice of it, preventing the whole array from being retained in memory.

sections.title: Same Characters, Two Different Objects in Memory
sections.content:
Writing `String s = "hello"` reuses a shared copy from the string pool, while `String s = new String("hello")` builds a brand-new object every time — same text, different object.

Why does this distinction exist at all? The literal form is the everyday way to make a string, and Java optimizes it by pooling. The `new String(...)` form is the generic 'construct an object' syntax, and like any `new`, it is contractually required to produce a fresh instance — so it can't reuse the pool.

How it plays out in memory: the literal `"hello"` goes into the **string pool**, and any other literal `"hello"` points at that same object. `new String("hello")` allocates a separate object on the general heap and copies the characters in. You now have two objects holding identical text at two different addresses.

That difference is invisible until you use `==`:

```java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");
System.out.println(a == b);      // true  — same pooled object
System.out.println(a == c);      // false — c is a separate object
System.out.println(a.equals(c)); // true  — same characters
```

The nuance: `==` returning `true` for two literals is an implementation detail you shouldn't lean on. The gotcha worth saying out loud — `new String("hello")` is almost never the right choice in real code; it just wastes memory. The one rare use is slicing a small string out of a huge `char[]` so the big array can be garbage-collected.

sections.title: Literal vs new String()
sections.content:
| | `String s = "hello"` | `String s = new String("hello")` |
|---|---|---|
| Where object lives | String pool (part of heap) | General heap |
| New object every time? | No — reuses pooled object if exists | Yes — always a new object |
| Memory efficiency | Better — shared for same content | Worse — duplicate objects possible |
| `==` with another literal | `true` if same content | `false` always |
| `.equals()` with other `"hello"` | `true` | `true` |
| When to use | Almost always | Rarely — avoid in normal code |

sections.title: Where Each One Lives: Pool vs Heap
sections.content:
Two literals share a single object in the pool; the constructor copies the characters into a separate object on the general heap. The arrows show what each variable actually points to. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["s1 = hello"] --> H B["s2 = hello"] --> H C["s3 = new String(hello)"] --> N subgraph POOL["String Pool (inside heap)"] H["hello
one shared object"] end subgraph HEAP["General Heap"] N["hello
separate new object"] end N -.->|"copies characters from"| H ``` Because `s1` and `s2` land on the same pooled object, `s1 == s2` is `true`. `s3` is a distinct object, so `s1 == s3` is `false` while `s1.equals(s3)` stays `true`.

sections.title: Proving the Memory Difference with ==
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting `==` to be `true` for a literal and a `new String`** — they hold the same characters but are different objects, so `==` is `false`; this is the single most common `String` bug for freshers.
- **Reaching for `new String("...")` to 'make a copy'** — it copies pointlessly; literals are already safe to share because `String` is immutable, so the copy buys you nothing but wasted memory.
- **Assuming strings from input, files, or concatenation are pooled** — only literals and explicitly `intern()`-ed strings live in the pool; a value read at runtime is a fresh heap object, so `==` against a literal fails.
- **Thinking `.equals()` and `==` are interchangeable** — `.equals()` compares characters and is what you almost always want; `==` compares object identity and happens to work for literals by accident.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`new` always means a new object** — `new String("hello")` is contractually a fresh heap instance, so it can never return a pooled object, while the literal `"hello"` reuses the pooled one.
- **`==` is `true` for two literals, `false` for literal vs `new`** — both hold `"hello"`, but `==` compares addresses, and only the literals share an address.
- **`.equals()` is `true` in every case where the characters match** — it ignores how the object was built, which is exactly why it's the correct content comparison.
- **The literal is more memory-efficient** — one shared object per unique text versus a guaranteed duplicate with `new`.
- **`new String()` is almost never justified** — the only real use is slicing a short string from a large `char[]` so the big backing array becomes garbage-collectable.
- **You rarely control how a `String` was created** — values from user input, files, or method returns may or may not be pooled, so depending on `==` is a latent bug; always use `.equals()`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Both expressions give you a string containing `"hello"` — the difference is where that object lives, and that quietly changes how `==` behaves. The literal form goes through the **string pool**: Java keeps one shared copy, so two literal `"hello"` variables point at the same object and `==` between them is `true`. The `new String("hello")` form is different — `new` is obligated to build a fresh object on the heap, so even though the text is identical, it's a separate object and `==` against the literal comes back `false`.

That `false` is exactly where candidates get burned: they compare a literal to a `new String` with `==`, expect `true`, and get a bug that's painful to track down. The fix is the rule everyone should internalize — compare string content with **`.equals()`**, not `==`. `==` is asking 'is this literally the same object?', which is almost never the question you actually have.

Honestly, in real code you should basically never write `new String("hello")`; it just creates a redundant object that wastes memory. The one genuinely useful case I'd mention is pulling a small substring out of a very large `char[]` so the huge backing array can be garbage-collected. So my take: default to literals, treat `new String` as a **code smell** unless you have that specific reason, and always reach for `.equals()` when comparing content.

questions.question: What happens internally when you concatenate strings with the + operator in Java?
questions.title: How Java's + Operator Works for Strings
questions.direct_answer: The `+` operator for Strings is syntactic sugar. For a single-line expression like `'a' + 'b' + 'c'`, the Java compiler rewrites it as a `StringBuilder` chain at compile time. For runtime concatenation in loops or with variables, a new StringBuilder is created per `+` operation, which creates a new String object each time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that + on Strings is not a primitive operation — the compiler transforms it, but only in a limited way that can produce O(n²) behavior in loops.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the compiler always optimises String + into a StringBuilder, including inside loops. The compiler can only see single expressions — not loop iteration sequences.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that since Java 9, the JVM uses a more dynamic concatenation strategy via invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory) which can be even more efficient than a classic StringBuilder chain — but the key interview point is still: use StringBuilder explicitly in loops.

sections.title: Why `+` on Strings Quietly Becomes a StringBuilder — Until a Loop Ruins It
sections.content:
When you join strings with `+`, the Java compiler quietly rewrites it into `StringBuilder` calls behind the scenes — there is no real string-add instruction in Java.

Why the rewrite? Strings are immutable, so 'adding' two of them can't change either one; it has to build a third. Doing that naively for `a + b + c` would create throwaway intermediate strings, so the compiler optimises a single concatenation expression into one `StringBuilder` chain instead.

How it looks: a one-line expression like `"Hello, " + name + "!"` compiles to roughly `new StringBuilder().append("Hello, ").append(name).append("!").toString()` — **one builder, one final `String`**. Efficient.

The nuance — and the part interviewers are really probing — is that this optimisation stops at the boundary of a single expression. The compiler sees one statement at a time; it cannot reach across loop iterations.

The gotcha:

```java
String result = "";
for (String word : words) {
    result = result + word; // new StringBuilder AND new String every iteration
}
```

Each pass builds a fresh `StringBuilder` from the growing `result` and produces a new `String`. For N words that's N allocations and **O(n²)** total character copies. The fix is to hoist one `StringBuilder` outside the loop, `append()` inside it, and call `toString()` once at the end. Since Java 9 the compiler uses `invokedynamic` (StringConcatFactory) for the single-line case, but the loop trap is unchanged.

sections.title: Single-Line + vs Loop + — What the Compiler Actually Produces
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["\"a\" + \"b\" + \"c\"
(single expression)"] --> B["Compiler rewrites to:
new StringBuilder()
.append('a').append('b').append('c')
.toString()"] B --> C["One StringBuilder
One String result"] D["result = result + word
(inside loop)"] --> E["Each iteration:
new StringBuilder(result)
.append(word).toString()"] E --> F["New object every iteration
O(n²) copies total"] ```

sections.title: What the Compiler Does — and Where It Can't Help
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Believing the compiler optimises `+` inside loops** — it only rewrites a single expression; it cannot merge iterations, so `result = result + word` in a loop is genuinely O(n²), not the efficient `StringBuilder` chain people assume.
- **Using `String +=` to build large strings** — every `+=` allocates a new `StringBuilder` and a new `String`; for thousands of items this shows up as real CPU and GC pressure. Use one `StringBuilder`.
- **Calling `toString()` inside the loop** — even with a manual `StringBuilder`, materialising the string every iteration throws away the benefit; call `toString()` exactly once after the loop.
- **Assuming `StringBuffer` is the answer for performance** — `StringBuffer` is synchronized and slower; in single-threaded code (the common case) `StringBuilder` is the right choice.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`+` on Strings is compiler sugar** — there's no native string-add bytecode; the compiler rewrites it into `StringBuilder.append()` calls, so 'string addition' is really object construction.
- **A single-line `+` chain is already efficient** — `a + b + c` becomes one `StringBuilder` and one `toString()`; rewriting it by hand gains nothing.
- **`+` in a loop is O(n²)** — the compiler can't span iterations, so each pass rebuilds a `StringBuilder` from scratch and emits a new `String`; N items mean N allocations and quadratic copying.
- **The fix is one hoisted `StringBuilder`** — declare it before the loop, `append()` inside, `toString()` once after; that turns O(n²) back into O(n).
- **Java 9+ uses `invokedynamic` for the single-line case** — `StringConcatFactory` lets the JVM pick the concat strategy at runtime, often beating a hand-written `StringBuilder` chain — but the loop still needs an explicit one.
- **Prefer `StringBuilder` over `StringBuffer`** — `StringBuffer` is synchronized and slower; you only need it for the rare shared-across-threads builder.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The key thing to know is that `+` on strings isn't a real operation — the compiler rewrites it into `StringBuilder` work, because strings are immutable and 'adding' them actually means building a new one. For a single line like `"Hello, " + name + "!"`, the compiler turns the whole expression into one **`StringBuilder`** with a chain of `append()` calls and a single `toString()`. That's efficient, and you don't need to rewrite it yourself.

The trap is assuming that optimisation extends into loops. It doesn't. The compiler only sees one statement at a time, so it can't merge iterations. When you write `result = result + word` inside a loop, every single pass spins up a brand-new `StringBuilder`, copies the whole accumulated string into it, appends one word, and produces a new `String`. For N words that's quadratic — **O(n²)** character copies — and it's a classic source of slow code that looks innocent.

The fix is to create one `StringBuilder` before the loop, `append()` inside it, and call `toString()` just once at the end. One detail that stands out: since Java 9, the single-line case is handled by `invokedynamic` through `StringConcatFactory`, so the JVM can choose an even better strategy at runtime. But that doesn't rescue loops — so my rule is simple: `+` is fine for a single expression, but the moment concatenation is in a loop, reach for an explicit `StringBuilder`.
